Comprehensive experimental validation across three datasets (RealSR, DRealSR, DIV2K-Val) with diverse metrics (pixel/perceptual/no-reference), including proper ablations for each component
Achieves competitive results with best FID (103.97) and lowest LPIPS (0.2542) on RealSR, plus superior generalization on other datasets while maintaining single trainable model
Sound technical framework with clear mathematical formulation (SAD twin trajectories, TAR weighting, DTC decoupling) and well-documented implementation details for reproducibility
Any-step sampling capability provides practical inference flexibility without retraining, with visual improvements in detail/texture quality across sampling steps
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Self-adversarial distillation adapted from concurrent text-to-image work (TwinFlow, FACM); dual-branch conditioning follows OmniControl; primary contribution is domain adaptation rather than methodological innovation

TAR design lacks theoretical justification—weight function w(s)=(1-s)²/s appears ad-hoc without ablation of alternatives; ablation shows TAR decreases FR metrics (PSNR 25.52→24.83) contradicting its motivation; quality-perception tradeoff unexplained

Incomplete competitive advantage: On RealSR, OSEDiff achieves better PSNR (25.15 vs. 24.83) and SSIM (0.7341 vs. 0.7198); claimed 'best perceptual metrics' selectively highlight FID/LPIPS while NIQE increases; missing quantified training time/memory benchmarks

Counter-intuitive any-step sampling behavior not analyzed: Table 2 shows PSNR decreases with more steps (24.83→23.61 at 30-step), contradicting diffusion theory, but investigation absent; unclear when any-step provides practical benefit

Hybrid training design undermines pure distillation claims: Pixel-space supervision loss Ldata (Eq. 13) adds direct reconstruction supervision to z_fake, creating hybrid approach not fully distinguished from pure SAD; Ldata contribution not ablated

Incomplete ablations: SAD baseline not compared against; DTC ablation doesn't isolate dual-branch vs. timestep-decoupling contributions; Ldata necessity not validated; design choices (LoRA rank=128, frozen noise branch rationale) lack justification

Limited experimental scope: Evaluated only on ×4 upscaling; generalization to ×2, ×8 unclear; training on modest 94,991 images—scaling behavior unknown; recent concurrent methods (e.g., OMGSR) not compared

Presentation issues: Notation inconsistencies (s vs. t_tar interchangeably); small figure text obscures visual claims; efficiency improvements claimed 'significantly' without quantitative wall-clock time or memory profiles

strengths: Addresses practical training efficiency problem by eliminating multiple auxiliary models, enabling large-scale distillation on limited resources
Any-step sampling flexibility without retraining is a useful feature not emphasized in prior one-step SR methods
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple datasets (RealSR, DRealSR, DIV2K-Val), metrics (FR and NR), and SOTA comparisons
Competitive quantitative results: achieves best perceptual metrics on RealSR (LPIPS: 0.2542, FID: 103.97) with single trainable model vs OSEDiff's 3 models
Includes ablation studies validating DTC and TAR components with visual and quantitative evidence
High-quality visual results demonstrating effective handling of fine textures and structured content without halo artifacts
weaknesses: Critical gap: main claim of 'training-efficient' learning is not validated—paper provides no GPU memory usage, wall-clock training time, or computational cost comparisons between TEASR and OSEDiff despite this being the primary motivation

Any-step sampling results contradict claims: Table 2 shows FID increases from 103.97 (1-step) to 118.41 (30-step), PSNR/SSIM decrease with more steps, inconsistent with narrative of 'more natural results' with increased steps. Paper inadequately explains this metric tension

Limited technical novelty: Self-Adversarial Distillation adapted from TwinFlow/FACM [3,27], Decoupled Timestep Condition from OmniControl [32], with TAR being a simple loss reweighting function w(s)=(1-s)²/s lacking justification for this specific form

Time-Aware Rectification weighting is ad-hoc and under-justified: no ablation on alternative weighting functions, no theoretical justification for (1-s)²/s form, and paradoxically degrades PSNR when combined with DTC (Table 3: 25.52→24.83)

Incomplete design analysis: multiple composite losses (L_base, L_adv, L_data, L_rectify) combined without ablations on relative weights (λ_cons, λ_lpips) or sensitivity analysis; stop-gradient operations throughout never motivated

Dense and unclear method presentation: Section 3 introduces three components with intertwined losses making logical flow difficult to follow; Algorithm 1 insufficient to understand dual-branch DTC implementation at inference; notation inconsistencies (t vs τ)
Reproducibility concerns: Qwen-Image-2512 unavailable at submission time, no code release mentioned, incomplete hyperparameter specification, loss weights unspecified
Limited scope and generalization: all experiments on ×4 upsampling only—no evaluation on ×2, ×8, or other factors; failure modes and scenarios where method underperforms not discussed

Unresolved metric interpretation: when FR metrics decrease but NR metrics increase with more steps (Table 2), paper provides no guidance on which to trust or how practitioners should interpret this trade-off

strengths: Addresses practical bottleneck in diffusion-based SR: eliminates need for 2-3× memory overhead by maintaining only one trainable model, enabling large-scale DiT training (20B parameters) on single GPUs
Technically sound framework with clear mathematical formulation (Eqs. 1-13) for self-adversarial distillation with twin trajectories and DMD-based rectification
Well-designed components: Time-Aware Rectification (w(s) = (1-s)²/s) elegantly addresses noise-level-dependent signal reliability; Decoupled Timestep Condition preserves fine-grained information

Comprehensive experimental validation: three datasets, eight metrics (pixel, perceptual, distribution-level), detailed ablations isolating each component; achieves best perceptual metrics on RealSR (LPIPS: 0.2542, FID: 103.97)
Unique practical advantage: supports seamless any-step sampling (1-30 steps) within single model without retraining, providing flexibility for speed-quality trade-offs
Clear presentation with effective visual comparisons (Figures 2-4) and ablation studies demonstrating contribution of each component
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: directly adapts Self-Adversarial Distillation from TwinFlow [3] and FACM [27] (text-to-image generation); Real-ISR adaptations are engineering-focused rather than introducing fundamental new principles

Contradictory any-step sampling results unexplained: FR metrics degrade with more steps (PSNR: 24.83→23.61, SSIM: 0.7198→0.6837 from 1 to 30 steps), directly contradicting claims of 'progressively more natural details'; raises fundamental question about training-inference mismatch

Unsubstantiated technical design choices: TAR weight function w(s) = (1-s)²/s presented without justification or comparison to alternative schedules (linear, cubic, exponential); no sensitivity analysis to functional form

Overstated performance claims: OSEDiff achieves higher PSNR (25.15 vs 24.83) and SSIM (0.7341 vs 0.7198) on RealSR; TEASR's advantage is primarily training efficiency (1 vs 3 models), not unconditional quality superiority

Missing critical empirical comparisons: no actual memory reduction measurements (GB), wall-clock training time comparisons, inference speed benchmarks, or convergence analysis; single-architecture validation (Qwen-Image only)

Insufficient theoretical justification: no analysis of why any-step sampling works despite metric degradation; connection between SAD training and inference flexibility is empirical rather than theoretically grounded
Incomplete ablation studies: Table 3 only varies DTC and TAR; missing sensitivity analysis for loss weights (λ_cons, λ_lpips), LoRA hyperparameters, and stop-gradient design choices
Reproducibility concerns: no code/checkpoint availability mentioned; hyperparameter selection rationale undocumented; training details incomplete (convergence criteria, learning rate schedules)

Vague limitations acknowledging but not exploring fundamental challenges: 'multiple composite objectives within limited model capacity' trade-offs uncharacterized; 'independent control over fidelity/realism' stated as open question without investigation

strengths: Addresses genuine practical problems: Significantly reduces training memory overhead from ~395% (OSEDiff) to 15.6% over baseline, enabling 20B-parameter model training on single GPU. This practical impact is substantial and valuable.

Solid technical execution: Well-motivated design combining SAD (adapted from prior work), TAR (theoretically grounded in KL divergence), and DTC (cleanly decoupling temporal signals). Each component has clear justification and the overall pipeline is coherent.

Comprehensive experimental validation: Tests across multiple real-world datasets (RealSR, DRealSR, DIV2K-Val) with diverse metrics (full-reference: PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, DISTS, FID; no-reference: MUSIQ, MANIQA, NIQE). Includes ablation studies, loss curves, training stability visualizations, and detailed hyperparameter reporting.

Any-step flexibility with performance scalability: Single model supports 1-step to 30-step sampling with progressive quality improvement. Unlike fixed-step methods, this enables runtime trade-offs between speed and quality without retraining, addressing a real use case limitation.

Competitive or superior empirical results: Achieves best perceptual metrics on RealSR (LPIPS=0.2542, FID=103.97). Outperforms OSEDiff on generalization (DrealSR and DIV2K-Val) despite using only single model. Qualitative results demonstrate superior detail recovery and reduced artifacts.

Strong theoretical grounding for TAR: Derives weight function w(s)=(1-s)²/s from KL divergence minimization principles. Includes sensitivity analysis validating design choice over alternatives. Theoretical derivation in supplementary material is thorough.

Honest limitations discussion: Acknowledges trade-offs from optimizing multiple objectives in single model and notes open challenges regarding independent control of fidelity vs. realism within fixed steps.
weaknesses: Limited component-level novelty: Core techniques are adaptations of recent work—SAD from TwinFlow (Cheng et al. 2025), TAR motivation from TSD-SR (Dong et al. 2025), and DTC from OmniControl (Tan et al. 2025). While adapting to Real-ISR is non-trivial, the incremental novelty is moderate.

Marginal improvements on some metrics: OSEDiff achieves slightly higher PSNR/SSIM on RealSR (25.15 vs 24.83 PSNR). While TEASR wins on perceptual metrics, the overall advantage is not dramatic. Framing as 'outstanding performance' may overstate the gains.

Any-step capability presentation is somewhat misleading: Any-step sampling is expected from diffusion models trained with consistency objectives. The core novelty is training efficiency, not step flexibility. Supplementary clarifies this, but main paper framing could be more precise about what's actually novel.

TAR theoretical justification has gaps: While the KL divergence derivation is provided, it relies on several assumptions about flow-matching framework and score function relationships that could be more rigorously justified. Sensitivity analysis (Table 3) shows alternatives like w(s)=1-s also work reasonably well (LPIPS 0.2408 vs 0.2542), weakening the theoretical claim.

Incomplete experimental comparisons: No direct latency/throughput comparisons under identical hardware (Table 2 uses different backbones: 0.8B, 2B, 20B). Training memory is compared, but inference speed comparisons are needed for fair assessment. Limited analysis of failure modes or dataset-specific performance variations.

Notation and presentation issues: Uses both t and τ notation inconsistently. Figure 2 is visually complex and difficult to parse on first reading. The main technical contribution (DTC) merits clearer, earlier explanation. Some key details relegated to supplementary material.

Dependency on proprietary models: Training uses Qwen-Image (20B) which may not be readily available for reproduction. This limits reproducibility compared to using open-source models, potentially restricting follow-up work.

Missing sensitivity analyses: No ablation on LoRA rank effects, loss weight sensitivity (λ values), or inference GPU memory usage. NR metrics show inconsistent improvements with more steps (Table 3), suggesting potential trade-offs that aren't fully explored.

Limited generalization analysis: Experiments at 512×512 resolution. Real-world deployment involves varied image sizes and degradation types. No analysis of how method scales to higher resolutions or generalizes beyond training degradation distributions.

strengths: Addresses practical problem of training efficiency for large diffusion models with genuine utility (single-A100 training of 20B models)
Comprehensive experimental validation with multiple metrics, diverse baselines, and thorough supplementary analysis including loss curves and sensitivity studies
Practical any-step capability without retraining is genuinely useful compared to fixed-step methods
Clear presentation with well-structured algorithms and effective figures
Theoretical justification for TAR weight schedule derived from KL divergence/distribution matching principles
weaknesses: Limited fundamental novelty: SAD directly adapted from TwinFlow/FACM; TAR's core insight (noise-level dependence) shared with concurrent TSD-SR; DTC follows OmniControl's dual-branch design. Components are competent combinations of existing ideas rather than novel contributions.

Unfair comparisons: Claims of memory efficiency compare 20B model to 0.86B baseline, making metrics misleading. Quantitatively, TEASR underperforms OSEDiff on RealSR PSNR (24.83 vs 25.15) and SSIM (0.7198 vs 0.7341), contradicting 'outstanding performance' claims.

Critical missing ablation: No empirical validation of SAD component itself despite being a core contribution. Justification ('would degenerate to multi-step model') is insufficient for top-tier venue.

Concerning ablation results obscured: DTC alone achieves LPIPS 0.2335 vs. full model's 0.2542—adding TAR *worsens* fidelity. Sensitivity analysis shows constant weight w(s)=1 superior to theoretically optimal (1-s)²/s, contradicting core claims.

Quality degradation across steps unaddressed: Increasing from 1 to 30 steps decreases PSNR (-1.22), SSIM (-0.0361), and worsens LPIPS (+0.0371), contradicting 'more steps→better quality' narrative. One-step model is empirically best for fidelity; no honest discussion of this trade-off.

Overclaimed results: Abstract claims 'outstanding performance on restoration fidelity' despite OSEDiff achieving higher FR metrics on key benchmark. 'Consistently outperforms' contradicted by competitive/mixed results across DrealSR and DIV2K-Val.

Reproducibility concerns: Paper promises 'Code:' on p.2 but provides no URL. TAR weight schedule appears ad-hoc (Eq. 2 uses tan function with unexplained 2.5 constant). Loss weight schedules lack ablation.

Limited scope and generalization: Only 4x SR evaluated; performance at other scales unknown. Only real-world degradation tested; generalization to other inverse problems unexplored. Domain-specific contribution limits broader impact.
Hyperparameter justification absent: LoRA rank 128 not ablated. Stop-gradient operations' necessity unjustified. Robustness to loss weight choices unclear despite complex schedules (Eq. 2).

strengths: Significant practical training efficiency: 15.6% memory increase vs. 395% for competing methods (OSEDiff), enabling large-scale model distillation on single GPU

Well-motivated technical design: Self-Adversarial Distillation cleverly creates dual trajectories within one model; Decoupled Timestep Condition preserves fine-grained noise information; TAR has theoretical justification via KL divergence derivation

Comprehensive experimental validation: Multiple datasets (RealSR, DRealSR, DIV2K-Val), diverse metrics (8+ evaluation criteria), thorough comparisons with SOTA methods, detailed ablations showing each component's contribution

Unique any-step sampling flexibility: Supports 1-30+ inference steps without retraining, enabling dynamic speed-quality trade-offs; superior generalization across datasets (PSNR on DrealSR: 28.54 vs OSEDiff 27.92)

Strong perceptual quality results: Lowest LPIPS (0.2542) and FID (103.97) on RealSR; visually superior to SOTA in qualitative comparisons (Fig. 3) with natural details and artifact-free text/structure reconstruction

Clear presentation with thorough documentation: Well-organized paper, effective figures (especially Fig. 2), supplementary includes training algorithm, loss curves, theoretical derivations, enabling understanding and reproducibility
Addresses real practitioner pain point: Memory constraints preventing large-scale model fine-tuning; practical solution with measurable impact on research accessibility
weaknesses: Limited fundamental novelty: Self-adversarial distillation adapted from concurrent text-to-image works [3,28]; Decoupled Timestep Condition similar to existing dual-branch finetuning; TAR weight follows straightforwardly from DMD principles—contribution is primarily in combination rather than novel concepts

Quantitative metric trade-offs not fully justified: Table 4 shows adding TAR decreases PSNR (24.93→24.83) and SSIM while improving NR metrics; trade-off between FR and perceptual quality not clearly necessary or well-motivated; claims of 'superior restoration quality' need nuance

Unfair model capacity comparisons: OSEDiff uses SD2.1 (0.86B) while TEASR uses Qwen-Image (20B); Table 2 inference times across different backbones conflate method efficiency with architecture differences; should clearly attribute gains to larger foundation models

Any-step sampling benefits overstated: Modest metric improvements 1→30 steps (LPIPS 0.2542→0.2913 is degradation; MUSIQ 68.50→68.42 declines); qualitative differences in Fig. 4 subtle; Table 3 shows FR metrics decrease with steps contradicting claims of improved quality

Insufficient design choice justification: TAR sampling range U(0.05, 0.95) lacks ablation; loss weight schedule formula (Eq. 2) using tan with factor 2.5 appears arbitrary without sensitivity analysis; LoRA rank/alpha hyperparameters unjustified

Missing failure case and limitation analysis: Section 5 briefly mentions 'optimizing multiple composite objectives' challenge without concrete examples; no analysis of underperformance scenarios; when is single-model insufficient vs. multi-model?

Reproducibility gaps: Code link stated but not provided; VAE architecture not explicitly specified; exact degradation parameters not fully listed; training time (computational cost) on 2 A100s not reported for complete efficiency assessment

Weak theoretical justification for pixel-space loss: Why does L_data prevent z^fake collapse? Why does auxiliary pixel-domain supervision help fake trajectory learning? Mechanism insufficiently explained; stop-gradient operations crucial but underexplained in main text
